title: Which US state privacy laws require employee training?
description: A state by state check of which US comprehensive privacy laws mention employee training, read on official state sites, and duties that still need training.
shortAnswer: Of the comprehensive state privacy laws checked on official state sites, only California's CCPA expressly requires training: staff who handle privacy inquiries must know the law and how to route requests. Virginia, Colorado, Connecticut, Utah, Delaware, Iowa, Indiana, Kentucky, Maryland and Minnesota contain no training clause, but each requires reasonable administrative safeguards and processor confidentiality duties that are hard to meet without trained staff.
keyTakeaways: California is the only state checked whose privacy statute and regulations name training: Civil Code 1798.130(a)(6), 1798.135(c)(3) and 11 CCR 7100.
Ten other comprehensive laws read in full on official state sites contain no employee training requirement.
All ten require reasonable administrative, technical and physical data security practices, and most require processor contracts that bind each person processing data to a duty of confidentiality.
Minnesota goes furthest on governance: section 325M.18 requires documented privacy policies and procedures naming a chief privacy officer or equivalent.
Texas, Oregon, Tennessee, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Rhode Island and Florida were not verified for this page; check them before relying on the table for those states.
jurisdiction: United States (state comprehensive consumer privacy laws)
regulator: State attorneys general (Colorado Department of Law, Connecticut Attorney General, Virginia Attorney General and others); California Privacy Protection Agency and California Attorney General
appliesTo: Controllers and processors that meet a state law's applicability thresholds
Privacy, customer support, security and engineering staff who handle personal data or consumer requests
Vendors and contractors processing personal data under processor contracts

sections.heading: Do state privacy laws outside California require training?

blocks.text: Not in so many words. The laws checked for this page, modeled largely on Virginia's Consumer Data Protection Act, impose duties on controllers and processors but do not say "train your employees." California is the exception: its statute and regulations require that people handling consumer inquiries be informed of the requirements, and the regulations add a documented training policy for businesses at 10 million consumers. That duty is covered in detail on the [CCPA and CPRA training page](/regulations/ccpa-cpra-employee-training-requirements).

Absence of a training clause is not absence of a training need. Every law checked requires reasonable administrative safeguards, timely handling of consumer requests and, in most cases, confidentiality commitments from everyone who processes the data. An organization asked by an attorney general how it meets those duties will usually point to staff training as part of the answer.

sections.heading: Which common duties still depend on trained staff?

blocks.text: Three duties recur across the non California laws, and each is executed by people. Training is the practical control that makes them happen consistently.

items: **Reasonable administrative safeguards.** Virginia section 59.1-578 requires controllers to "establish, implement, and maintain reasonable administrative, technical, and physical data security practices," and Connecticut, Delaware, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Minnesota and Utah use the same or near identical wording. Administrative safeguards are the people side of security, which is where awareness training sits.

**Confidentiality of everyone who processes data.** Processor contracts in Virginia (59.1-579), Connecticut (42-521), Utah (13-61-301), Iowa (715D.5), Delaware (12D-107) and Minnesota (325M.13) must require that each person processing personal data is subject to a duty of confidentiality. A signed confidentiality term is stronger when staff understand what it covers.

**Consumer request handling.** Each law sets response deadlines, for example 90 days under Iowa's chapter 715D with one 45 day extension. Missed or mishandled requests are the most visible failures, and they usually trace back to front line staff who did not recognize a request.

blocks.text: Minnesota's documented policy requirement in section 325M.18 deserves separate attention. A written description of privacy policies and procedures with a named privacy lead is easier to defend when the organization can also show that the people bound by those procedures were trained on them. The general method is in [how to convert policies into training](/guides/how-to-convert-policies-into-training).

sections.heading: How should a multi state business design one training program?

blocks.text: Build to California and the strictest health data rules, then add state specific modules only where obligations genuinely differ. Most of the content, such as recognizing a privacy request, verifying identity, routing opt outs and protecting data, is the same in every state.

The design steps are in [how to build a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix).

sections.heading: Which state laws were not verified for this page?

blocks.text: Texas, Oregon, Tennessee, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Rhode Island and Florida were not verified, because their official legislature sites could not be read in full during this review. Their laws follow similar models, but this page does not state whether they contain training language. Treat those states as open items and read the statute on the official site before relying on any summary.

blocks.title: Federal overlay
blocks.text: Financial institutions subject to the FTC Safeguards Rule have an express federal training duty that applies regardless of state law. See [FTC Safeguards Rule employee training](/regulations/ftc-safeguards-rule-employee-training).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry represents each state duty, such as request deadlines, confidentiality and safeguards, as an obligation linked to shared concepts and roles. A single request handling competency can then satisfy California's explicit training rule and support the safeguard duties in other states, with the state specific differences kept visible.

faqs.q: If a state law has no training clause, can an attorney general still fault a business for poor training?
faqs.a: Indirectly, yes. Attorneys general enforce the duties in the statute, such as reasonable administrative safeguards and timely responses to consumer requests. If a violation traces to staff who did not know the procedure, the absence of training weakens the argument that the safeguards were reasonable. Training is evidence of compliance, even where it is not itself the obligation.

Colorado's rules mention trained personnel only as one option for verifying parental consent: a toll free number or videoconference staffed by trained personnel (Rule 7.06). Rule 6.09 requires reasonable administrative, technical, organizational and physical safeguards but does not name training. Organizations commonly list awareness training among their organizational safeguards.

faqs.q: Is a confidentiality agreement enough to meet the processor duty?
faqs.a: The Virginia model laws require processor contracts to ensure that each person processing personal data is subject to a duty of confidentiality, so a signed agreement is the core evidence. Pairing the agreement with short training on what the duty covers makes it more likely to be followed and gives the controller assurance when it oversees the processor.

faqs.q: Do these laws cover employee data?
faqs.a: Of the laws checked, Virginia, Connecticut, Delaware, Iowa, Indiana, Kentucky, Maryland and Minnesota define consumer to exclude an individual acting in a commercial or employment context, so their request handling duties focus on customers. California is different: its employment exemption became inoperative on January 1, 2023, so employee requests must be handled under the CCPA.
